title: When the Compass Turns
premise: Felix Nakamura has spent two decades as a contract surveyor in the remote delta country, keeping his famous archaeologist father's name off every permit and his own heart out of every camp. When a government survey team vanishes from a flooded tributary, Felix is the only guide willing to search, and he's forced to accept help from Mara Oduya, a hydrologist whose brother was on the missing team. As monsoon rains trap them on a leaking boat among drowned ruins, Felix realizes the team didn't vanish by accident—they found something his father spent his life hunting, and someone is willing to kill to keep it buried. Felix must choose between the anonymity he's built his life around and the truth that could finally let him belong to someone. In the end, Felix survives the flood, exposes the cover-up, and—having lost the boat, the ruins, and his old life—chooses to stay, letting the compass of his life finally point toward a home rather than away.
about_author: Juniper Iversen is the pen name of a former river surveyor who spent eleven seasons mapping waterways across three continents before turning to fiction. She writes adventure novels about people who measure their lives in distance rather than time.

chapters.title: Miles, Not Years
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Establishes Felix's solitary life as a freelance surveyor who takes jobs no one else wants and never stays anywhere longer than a season. A letter arrives from his estranged father's estate—his father has died, and left him an unopened field journal. Felix burns nothing but reads nothing, storing the journal in his gear bag. Emotional beat: grief he refuses to name, and the habit of leaving before attachment forms.

chapters.title: The Empty Landing
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. A government liaison hires Felix to retrace a survey team's route on the Serevan tributary after they miss two check-ins. At their last camp Felix finds gear neatly stowed, a cold cookfire, and no tracks in the mud—impossible after four days of rain. He also finds a survey marker stamped with his father's initials, decades old. Emotional beat: unease curdling into dread; the past has followed him into the wilderness.

chapters.title: A Stranger's Oar
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara Oduya intercepts Felix at the supply depot, having bribed her way onto the search as a 'hydrological consultant.' Her brother Emeka was the survey team's leader. She doesn't trust Felix—his name is on none of the permits, and she's heard rumors he works for the other side. They strike a brittle bargain: she pays, he pilots. Emotional beat: two guarded people forced into proximity, friction masking fear.

chapters.title: Water Over Stone
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. They travel upriver ahead of the monsoon's first wall of rain, and Mara's expertise saves them from a false channel that would have stranded them. In the evenings, Felix deflects her questions about his father, the renowned archaeologist Dr. Kenji Nakamura. She notices he flinches at the name. Emotional beat: grudging respect forming; Felix realizes invisibility is harder to maintain with a witness aboard.

chapters.title: The Drowned City
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. They find the missing team's second camp—and Emeka's journal, waterproofed and hidden, describing a submerged stone complex the floodwaters have exposed for the first time in a century. The final entry is cut off mid-sentence. That night the monsoon arrives in earnest, and their boat's hull, holed by submerged debris, begins to leak. Emotional beat: wonder and terror braided together; discovery has a cost, and the rain is collecting.

chapters.title: What the River Keeps
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Bailing water through the storm, Mara reads Emeka's journal aloud by flashlight and learns he'd found evidence the site was being stripped by a private crew with government cover—someone on the survey team was a plant. She confronts Felix about who he really is, and he finally tells her: the son who walked away. Emotional beat: the walls come down; confession as survival, because a leaking boat forgives no secrets.

chapters.title: The Other Boat
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The salvage crew finds them—a gunmetal skiff, no markings, led by a man named Voss who claims to be rescue. Felix recognizes the survey equipment in Voss's hold: it belongs to the missing team. A tense standoff on the flooded water; Mara plays the grieving sister while Felix signals their position to a passing barge. Voss lets them go—but follows. Emotional beat: cold fear sharpening into resolve; they are witnesses now, and witnesses are cargo.

chapters.title: Running the Flood
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. A night chase down the swollen tributary, Felix running rapids that exist only during monsoon while Mara navigates by Emeka's hand-drawn charts. The boat is dying beneath them; they take shelter in the exposed ruin itself, a stone chamber above the flood line, and discover the missing survey team's fate—three survivors, hiding, kept alive by the looters who need their silence. Emotional beat: hope and horror in the same breath; the missing are found, but not safe.

chapters.title: Compass Points
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The climax. Felix uses his father's field journal—finally opened—to prove the site's true location and significance, broadcasting the evidence via the survivors' satellite phone before Voss can cut them off. In the confrontation on the flooded causeway, Felix nearly drowns saving Emeka, and Mara pulls them both from the water. Voss's crew scatters as the barge arrives with authorities. Emotional beat: Felix chooses, for the first time, to stand in the light rather than vanish—survival finally means more than escaping.

chapters.title: Where the Water Settles
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, closing with Felix's. Weeks later: the survivors testify, the salvage operation is exposed, and Felix reads his father's last journal page—an apology, and a request that he stop running. Mara asks him to stay through the dry season to help document the site properly. Felix unpacks a bag he has kept ready to leave for twenty years, and doesn't repack it. Emotional beat: quiet resolution; belonging isn't found, it's chosen, and the compass finally rests.
